utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, good afternoon to you. If you could call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, good afternoon to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I can hear you and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And you may sit down. General Talic, good afternoon to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I can hear you in a language that I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. General Talic, you may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Anna Richterova and Julian Nicholls for the Prosecution, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, madam, and good afternoon to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm Milan Trbojevic. Lead counsel for Mr. Brdjanin is present, Mr. John Ackerman; and our assistant Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good afternoon to you. Appearances for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic and Natasha Ivanovic-Fauveau for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Good afternoon to you. Now, before we -- yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution filed their designation of 92 bis, and I can respond orally if that's acceptable to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was going to bring -- draw your attention to it, because I was informed rightly or wrongly, I don't know, that your time limit had lapsed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'll do whatever you want me to do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No go -- go ahead. Unless there is an objection from the Prosecution. But in any case, I would grant you an extension of a few minutes to respond to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we accept with regard -- and agree to 92 bis with regard to the following.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait. One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you ready?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You agree to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. 7.163, 7.107, 7.191. They were numbered improperly in the Prosecution's annex, Your Honour, so the numbers I'm giving you are the correct ones. And then we oppose 7.101, 7.117, unless they're brought here for cross-examination. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. And from General Talic's part, we have received the -- your document. It's still in French. I have gone through it very briefly. We'll wait for the English translation to be a hundred per cent sure that I have read it well, and then we'll come down with a decision pretty soon, I would suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If the Court pleases, may I inform the Court that we have filed the motion today as -- as we promised yesterday about the closed session as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. That hasn't been brought to our attention as of yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was filed just a couple of hours ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So I thank you both.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I must apologise, but when we filed that motion we made two errors in numberings. When we submitted the list of our witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: -- we made the corrections. So I only want to make it clear that the witness who was filed under number 7.117 is in reality 7.107. And the witness who was filed under 7.107 is in reality 7.106.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go into private session and I'll say names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Inneke, please could you ask my secretary to bring me back the lists of witnesses I had in my green file for Kljuc municipality, the one which was filed yesterday. And tell her to leave it always there. I told her, but it doesn't seem -- it seems to go in from one ear straight out through the next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Richterova, I think one --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I must apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You've mixed -- you've mixed it up.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes. I've completely mixed it up. You are right. And I apologise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. According to my records, what was 7.107 --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: -- is in reality 7.117.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Becomes 7.117.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes. And what was 7.106 is 7.107.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which mixes things up. Mr. Ackerman, bear with me, please. And Mr. Zecevic, do take note - and Madam Fauveau - of what I'm going to say, because it may have a bearing on your response, in as far as each of the witnesses were indicated, because this may -- may change something. I have it here you had submitted first as 7.106 a certain witness under the Rule 92 bis rule. Okay? 7.106 I am told now becomes 7.107. But 7.106 -- when you say 7.107, you were referring to the new 7.107, Mr. Ackerman. No? According to yesterday's list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. What -- this is getting beyond -- I think for the record we should go to private session and let me say the names of the ones that I oppose for 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So there's no confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go to private session, please, because otherwise we are getting confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I promised you yesterday two things on behalf of the Chamber. One was that we would take up the matter of the way sittings were being proposed starting from August till December, namely in relation to what appeared to be a preponderance of sittings in the afternoon -- sittings in the afternoon. We have brought that up -- we have studied it, going back to January, to when we started the trial, and making a sort of a comparative exercise with the other five pending cases, and we have brought the matter up with who we thought we ought to bring it. There will -- I expect -- there will be some kind of response later on. I'm pretty sure there will be some adjustments to the timetable as -- as it shows now, some amendments to it, also because there are some obvious mistakes. I mean, for example, Stakic first -- last week of August, Stakic appears twice and at the same time sitting 12 -- sitting 10 times in one week but always in the same time, from 9.00 to quarter to 2.00. We have obviously been omitted in one particular week, and Martinovic case has been duplicated in that week. So there are some mistakes. But apart from those -- from the rectification of those mistakes, there is going to be some adjustment to the timetable, which we will report back to you the moment or as soon as practicable after we get the final response. That's number one. Second, you will recall, Mr. Ackerman, Mr. Zecevic, that you had asked more or less sittings to be -- to take place on a four-weeks on, one-week off pattern, which was objected to by the Prosecution. That basically meant that you were asking for three breaks before the Christmas recess, which included one week that we had indicated to you. The Prosecution was preferring a nine weeks on, one week off, and that would have meant two breaks, including the one which we were suggesting to you. We have studied it carefully. More or less the situation -- the position seems to be the following: That we have not been working on a basis of four weeks on, one week off, but we also haven't been working on a basis of nine weeks on and one week off. More or less we have been pretty much flexible, inserting a break where we thought it would be fit and proper to. And what we are proposing to you is that we will have between now and the Christmas recess two breaks which, however, will be longer than the usual week. In other words, the way we are approaching it is the way we have approached it in the past. We will take a Friday before the Saturday, which will give you the benefit of three more days -- two full weekends plus a Friday before, which would make it to a total of ten days off, and that will be the first one. The second one will start on a Saturday and will finish on a Monday; in other words, we will start on a Tuesday, which would again give you a ten-day break -- give you and us. I mean, it's -- so the position is as follows: The breaks will be on -- we will resume on the 26th of August, as you know. We will then have practically five full weeks - five full weeks - but we will stop for a break on the 27th of September, which is a Friday, resuming on the 7th of October. In other words, the break will be from the 27th of September till the 6th of October, both days included - both days included - we will be issuing a scheduling order in due course. Then we will be sitting for six full weeks, and we will have a break from the 9th of November through the 18th of November, both days included. Then we will sit for three and a half weeks, at the end of which we'll have the Christmas recess. And that, I think, strikes a balance between the respective positions that had been taken. This works out as follows, actually, that between you -- excluding Saturdays and Sundays - excluding Saturdays and Sundays, I'm not counting those - between now and the last day of the year, the 31st of December, there are technically 92 working days - 92 working days - of which one is a UN holiday, two are taken for plenary, four for court maintenance, 12 recess -- official recess, 12 break -- days off that we are allowing, and that would bring us to a total of sitting days of 61, which more or less is -- corresponds to what the other Trial Chambers will be having. Actually, it's a little -- even a little bit less than what the other Chambers will be having. So that's the situation: 92 days, of which 61 will be working days, sitting days, 12 break, 12 recess, four court maintenance, two plenary, one UN holiday. All right? We will be issuing the appropriate scheduling order later on during the week. I hope that is satisfactory. I think now we will need to prepare the room for the closed session. Yes, please. We'll move into a closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
